title: A worker container's harness budget is 30 minutes, which is shorter than a real tick takes
description:
Found by the first cloud run in which per-tick containers actually worked (run_2e66e765f74c4192b2b9a24a6e8415cf, 2026-08-22, epic 72y, ticks 201/5jo/5qj).

All three containers booted green, drove the omp loop on deepseek-v4-flash competently — 393+ model calls with real tool use, 95-99% prompt cache — and were then KILLED mid-work. Each pushed only a ticks-worker-generated report:

  harness omp exited 124, 0 work commit(s), 0 uncommitted path(s)
  STATUS: BLOCKED — the harness exited 124 and wrote no report; re-dispatch this tick

Exit 124 is a timeout kill. cloud/factory/src/run-workflow.ts:1505 sets CLOUD_WAVE_WAIT_TIMEOUT_MS = 30 * 60_000, and workerHarnessTimeoutSeconds derives TICKS_WORKER_TIMEOUT from it minus WORKER_PUSH_MARGIN_MS — so every worker gets ~29 minutes of harness time no matter what the tick is or what the run's own --max-wall-clock says.

That budget contradicts this repo's own measurements. Tick y45 recorded a COMPLETE one-tick epic at 78 minutes on deepseek-v4-pro, and flash takes more steps than pro for the same work. Thirty minutes is not a safety margin, it is a guarantee that any non-trivial tick is killed just before it commits — which is the most expensive possible failure, because the run pays for all the work and keeps none of it.

Note the two bounds are doing different jobs and should not be one constant: the WAVE wait is how long the supervisor waits before reconciling, and the HARNESS bound is how long the agent may work. Today the second is derived from the first, so raising the agent's budget also lengthens every supervisor observation.

Work:
1. Raise the default materially — 78 minutes was a complete epic, so a single tick's budget should be at least that. Justify the number from measurement, not taste.
2. Derive it from the RUN's --max-wall-clock when the operator set one, rather than a constant that ignores it. A run given 90m should not kill its workers at 29m.
3. Keep the push margin: a worker must still bound itself under the dispatcher so it pushes what it has rather than being destroyed with it. The margin is the mechanism that turns a timeout into a legible branch, and it worked exactly as designed here — that part is not broken.
4. Consider whether a killed worker's partial work should be committed rather than discarded. All three of these containers had done substantial real work.

acceptance_criteria: A worker's harness budget derives from the run's wall-clock allowance rather than a fixed 30 minutes, with a default justified by measurement; a tick that takes an hour completes and pushes work commits. Proven by a live run, not only a unit test.
closed_reason: Completed: a worker's harness budget now derives from the run's REMAINING wall clock, capped by the deployment, defaulting to 90m — justified by y45's measured 78-minute complete one-tick epic on the faster-stepping v4-pro. Also found and fixed a second clamp that would have defeated a code-only fix: wrangler.toml's RUN_MAX_WALL_CLOCK_MS was 45m, so run_2e66e765's --max-wall-clock 90m was silently clamped before the 30-minute constant even applied. The derivation is inverted — the agent's budget is now the decision and the supervisor's patience follows it.
